corrected_draft.description_long: An SEC Schedule 13D amendment filed by Vivek Ramaswamy and other reporting persons states that he beneficially owned 5,693,897 Strive, Inc. shares, representing 8.4% of the class under the filing’s stated assumption that Class B shares convert to Class A. The filing identifies April 20, 2026 as the event date. It explains that Strive’s at-the-market share sales increased the number of outstanding shares, causing the reporting group to fall below the 50% voting-power threshold in its shareholder agreement. The agreement then terminated automatically, and the reporting persons ceased to constitute a group. The amendment says Ramaswamy still beneficially owned more than 5% and would report separately; the other exiting persons fell below 5%. This establishes an ownership disclosure and reporting change. It does not support the held entry’s claim of a 7.6% stake as of May 28, nor any assertion that his Ohio policy platform was designed to benefit Strive investors.

corrected_draft.title: DOJ Challenges Maryland Court’s Automatic Immigration Injunctions
corrected_draft.description_short: On June 25, 2025, DOJ announced a complaint challenging a Maryland court standing order that automatically enjoined some immigration removals.
corrected_draft.description_medium: On June 25, 2025, the Justice Department announced that it had filed a complaint against the U.S. District Court of Maryland over a standing order requiring automatic injunctions when detained people filed habeas petitions. DOJ said the order blocked removal or challenges to their legal status and characterized the practice as judicial overreach. The release documents a legal challenge, not a refusal to obey court orders.
corrected_draft.description_long: On June 25, 2025, the Justice Department announced that it had filed a complaint against the U.S. District Court of Maryland concerning the court’s standing order on immigration habeas petitions. According to DOJ’s release, the order instructed the court clerk to automatically enter an injunction against removing or challenging the legal status of a person detained in Maryland who filed a habeas petition. The department argued that the standing order conflicted with the requirements for preliminary injunctions and with Supreme Court precedent. Attorney General Pamela Bondi said that injunctions had impeded President Trump’s agenda and described the Maryland order as judicial overreach. The public statement documents DOJ’s formal challenge to a specific court procedure and its criticism of the judiciary. DOJ described the complaint as its latest action against what it called unlawful judicial overreach. It does not establish that Bondi refused to enforce multiple injunctions, as the original entry claimed.

corrected_draft.title: State Department Orders Social Media Vetting for Visa Applicants Who Have Been to Gaza
corrected_draft.description_short: On April 17, 2025, the State Department ordered social-media vetting for visa applicants who had been in Gaza on or after January 1, 2007.
corrected_draft.description_medium: On April 17, 2025, the State Department directed U.S. diplomatic missions to conduct social-media vetting for immigrant and nonimmigrant visa applicants who had been in Gaza since January 1, 2007. Reuters reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed the cable. This is a narrower and better-supported event than the entry’s claim that DHS revoked visas simply for posts critical of Israel; the cable concerned screening and security review, not a blanket automatic revocation rule.
corrected_draft.description_long: On April 17, 2025, the State Department ordered U.S. diplomatic and consular posts to conduct social-media vetting for immigrant and nonimmigrant visa applicants who had been in the Gaza Strip on or after January 1, 2007. Reuters reported the directive from an internal cable signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The cable instructed that potentially derogatory security information found in an online review should prompt a security advisory opinion. Reuters also reported that the administration had revoked hundreds of visas in other cases and that officials had cited foreign-policy concerns involving some student visa holders. Those broader actions do not show that DHS revoked visas across the board because applicants had posted criticism of Israel. The corrected entry should identify the State Department’s Gaza-related screening directive, preserve its applicant scope and date, and avoid merging it with separate visa-revocation cases or attributing it to DHS.

corrected_draft.title: Appeals court keeps DOJ subpoenas to Letitia James's office blocked
corrected_draft.description_short: Appeals court keeps DOJ subpoenas to Letitia James's office blocked
corrected_draft.description_medium: On August 21, 2026, the Second Circuit upheld a block on Justice Department subpoenas seeking records from New York Attorney General Letitia James's office about litigation involving Trump, his family business, and the NRA. The court found that John Sarcone, the Trump ally overseeing the probe, had served unlawfully. The Justice Department disagreed and said it would seek Supreme Court review.
corrected_draft.description_long: A divided Second Circuit panel on August 21, 2026, upheld an order blocking Justice Department subpoenas seeking records from New York Attorney General Letitia James’s office. The subpoenas concerned the office’s litigation against Donald Trump, his family business, and the National Rifle Association. Reuters reported that the court found John Sarcone, the Trump ally overseeing the investigation, had served unlawfully, supporting the block on the subpoenas. The panel’s ruling concerned the prosecutor’s authority and the subpoenas; it did not decide every allegation involved in the underlying matters. The Justice Department disagreed with the decision and said it would seek review by the Supreme Court. The event is an appellate ruling about the legal authority behind these investigative subpoenas, not a final resolution of all disputes between James and Trump or a finding about the merits of each underlying case. Other claims in the underlying litigation were not decided by this ruling.
